title: Lord of the sabbath (Mark 2:23–28)
hook: the disciples pick grain on the sabbath, and Jesus defends them

segments.voice: Yesterday, a wedding, a patched coat and a wineskin: new wine, new skins. Did one old thing get done a new way? Day one hundred sixty-six.

A Saturday in Galilee, early summer. The grain is high on both sides of a footpath. Jesus and his friends are walking through, and they're hungry, so as they go, the disciples reach out, pull off a few heads of grain, rub them in their hands and eat. Anyone could do that; the law of Moses allowed a passerby to pick by hand from a neighbor's field. The trouble is the day. It's the sabbath, the day of rest, and some Pharisees watching say picking grain is harvesting, and harvesting is work. Why are they doing what isn't allowed? Jesus answers them. Today: Lord of the sabbath.
screen: `A PATH THROUGH THE GRAIN.` → `HUNGRY HANDS.` → `BUT IT'S THE SABBATH.`

segments.voice: It helps to know how much the sabbath mattered, and still matters. It's the fourth of the Ten Commandments: one day in seven, no work, for everyone, including servants, foreigners and animals. For Jews it was, and is, a gift and a sign of belonging to God, kept with real joy. So the Pharisees' question is serious, not petty. What counts as work is exactly what careful people argued about. Jesus answers first from scripture. Remember David, he says, when he and his men were hungry, and the priest gave them the holy bread from the house of God, bread only priests were meant to eat. Need came first. Then the line some of you met back on day one hundred twenty-three, in the old King James Bible: "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath." And then one more sentence, the one that makes today's title: "Therefore the Son of man is Lord also of the sabbath." Son of Man is the name Jesus most often uses for himself in the gospels. So this isn't only a ruling about grain. Christians hear him claiming the right to say what the day of rest is for. And a neighbor shares the first half. Jewish teachers also taught that saving a life outweighs the sabbath, and one early rabbinic teaching says something very close: the sabbath is given to you, not you to the sabbath. Most Christians now keep Sunday, the day of the resurrection, as their day of rest and worship. Some, like Seventh-day Adventists, keep Saturday. Either way the question stays the same: is my rest healing me?
screen: `ONE DAY IN SEVEN, FOR EVERYONE.` · `DAVID AND THE HOLY BREAD.` · `THE SABBATH WAS MADE FOR MAN.` · `LORD ALSO OF THE SABBATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest in a way that heals. Settle, and let your shoulders drop. Ask your body what kind of tired it is. Sleepy tired, needing a nap. People tired, needing quiet. Screen tired, needing a window and some sky. Worried tired, needing to put something down. Don't solve it. Just name it. Then choose one small rest that fits that tiredness, for later today. If you pray, you can rest these two minutes in God's company. If you don't, rest them anyway. The bell holds the time.
Lord of the sabbath. Jesus's claim, in a grain field, to say what the day of rest is for: people, not the other way around.
Your line: made for people. Today, when a rule or a routine starts grinding someone down, you included, ask what it was made for. Day one hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Most Christians keep Sunday as a day of worship and rest in honor of the resurrection, while some churches, such as Seventh-day Adventists, keep the seventh day, Saturday, as the sabbath.

original.note: Greek, from the Hebrew shabbat: to stop, to rest.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus didn't care about the sabbath.
what it means: he defends hungry friends and says the day of rest was made for people, then claims to be its Lord.
what a scholar hears: Mark 2:27 is close to an early rabbinic saying, and 1 Samuel names the priest Ahimelech, not Abiathar as Mark does.

notes: Deuteronomy 23:25 permits plucking ears by hand in a neighbor's field; confirm.

The rabbinic parallel ('the sabbath is given to you, not you to the sabbath') is usually cited from the Mekhilta on Exodus 31:14, attributed to R. Simeon ben Menasya; paraphrased. Confirm the reference and that the 'neighbor' framing is respectful.
Mark 2:26 names Abiathar; 1 Samuel 21 names Ahimelech. A known puzzle mentioned only in the trapdoor; confirm Keepers are comfortable including it.
Day 123 taught Mark 2:27 ('Made for you'); the teach refers back to it.
Sunday vs. Saturday observance stated without ranking; confirm.
